SECTION 3. 
AsSIGNMENTS OF RIGHTS 
This chapter addresses a variety of situations 
in which a third 
person has rights or responsibilities with respect to a contract entered 
into between two other parties. First, Section 1 addresses the concept of 
third-party beneficiaries. Second, Section 2 addresses delegation of a 
party's duties pursuant to a contract. 
In this 
section, we address 
a third multi-party 
situation-
transactions in which a contract party to whom performance is owed (the 
"obligee" with respect to that duty) transfers (or "assigns") to a third 
party (the "assignee") the right of the obligee (now also the "assignor") to 
receive performance from the other party to the contract (the "obligor" 
with respect to that performance). A number of issues are raised by such 
assignments. Most prominent is the question of wh<•ther the result of the 
assignment is that the obligor's duty is now owed to the assignee (and, 
thus, if the obligor does not satisfy the duty whether the assignee has a 
claim against the obligor). Other issues include rules covering how an 
assignment is made, defenses the obligor can raise agamst the assignee, 
and the extent to which the assignee's rights are effective against third 
parties. 
Not surprisingly, this third-party aspect of contracts is exceedingly 
complicated. Indeed, a major portion of it is governed by other law that 
is beyond the scope of this course. In particular, with a few exceptions 
that are 
not material to this 
discussion, a major category of 
assignments-assignment 
of an obligee's right to be paid money by the 
obligor-is treated by the law as a "secured transaction'' and is governed 
by Article 9 of the Uniform Commercial Code. This section addresses only 
briefly the rules of Article 9 that apply to such assignments, with more 
detailed analysis left for a course that covers secured transactions. From 
time to time, however, we will confront Article 9 vocabulary, in which the 
obligee/assignor is a "debtor," the assignee is a "secured party," and the 
obligor is an "account debtor." 
Illustration 3 to Restatement § 334 presents an example that serves 
as a good place to start our analysis of assignments. In that illustration, 
"B contracts with A to furnish A's family with all the oil it shall need for 
the ensuing year at a fixed price." Then "A assigns his rights under the 
contract to C." This simple tale raises a slew of questions. Is A permitted
